title: Look again
hookLine: look at the sky again and again: do you see any flaw (67:3–4)

lines: WHEN DID YOU LAST LOOK UP?
cards: When did you last look at the sky on purpose? Not to check the weather on the way to the car. Not a sunset photo for someone else.
Just looked, and kept looking, from a bus window or a back step or a parking lot. The third verse of al-Mulk doesn't describe the sky and move on. It gives the reader an assignment.
Look. Then look again. Then once more.
Go ahead and try to find a flaw.

teach.b: Verse three says Allah created seven heavens, one above another, tibaqan, in layers. Then, in Pickthall: "Thou (Muhammad) canst see no fault in the Beneficent One's creation; then look again: Canst thou see any rifts?"
Fault translates tafawut: a mismatch, a seam that doesn't line up. Rifts translates futur: cracks, splits, gaps. So the question is: anywhere up there, does it fall apart?
Look again, twice more, karratayn, and your sight will come back to you worn out and dim, having found nothing. It's a dare the verse expects you to lose. You can look until your eyes ache.
Notice what the verse isn't saying. It doesn't ask you to stop looking because the answer is already known.
It asks you to keep looking, again and again, because the looking is the point. The Qur'an asks this kind of question elsewhere too: do they not see, do they not reflect.

Some Muslim readers have taken these verses as an invitation to study the natural world, the night sky included. Astronomers in Muslim lands tracked the stars, partly to fix prayer times and the direction of Mecca.

But this verse doesn't need an observatory. It needs a window, or a patch of sky above a parking lot, and the patience to look a second time, when your eyes start to see what they skipped the first time.

how: Muslims read 67:3–4, often nightly as part of al-Mulk, as an invitation to contemplate creation (tafakkur); astronomers in Muslim lands studied the sky, partly to set prayer times and the direction of Mecca.

o: look once, and trust the answer you have
look away from the sky, and don't question
look at creation again and again for a flaw

p: a mismatch, a seam that doesn't fit

s: the verse tells the reader not to question the sky
it dares the reader to look again and again for a flaw.
the eye comes back worn out and dim, having found no flaw
that's verse four's answer to its own challenge.
astronomers in Muslim lands watched the sky partly for prayer times
the times and the direction of Mecca depend on the sky.

games.q: you've looked at the sky once for any crack or flaw. what does verse four tell you to do next?
games.why: look again, twice more. your sight comes back worn out and dim, having found no rift.

practice: If you can see the sky, even through a window, look at it now; if not, close your eyes and picture the last sky you saw. First look: take in the whole thing, color, light, any cloud, then close your eyes for a breath.
Second look, slower: find one thing you missed, an edge of cloud, a bird, the way the blue changes near the ground, and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Look again. In 67:3–4 the Qur'an invites the reader to look at the sky, then again and again, for any mismatch or crack, and come back worn out. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic, 67:3: so turn your sight back, look again.

carryVoice: Your line: the looking is the point. The second look finds what the first one missed. Day six hundred thirty-eight.
